claim: CRISPR-Cas systems provide sequence-specific immunity against phages and mobile genetic elements using CRISPR-associated nucleases guided by short CRISPR RNAs (crRNAs).
source: CRISPR-Cas systems provide sequence-specific immunity against phages and mobile genetic elements using CRISPR-associated nucleases guided by short CRISPR RNAs (crRNAs).
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field supported by the manuscript's introduction and references to prior work.

claim: Type III systems exhibit a robust immune response that can lead to the extinction of a phage population.
source: Type III systems exhibit a robust immune response that can lead to the extinction of a phage population, a feat coordinated by a multi-subunit effector complex that destroys invading DNA and RNA.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the manuscript to prior work (Bari et al., 2017; Pyenson et al., 2017).

claim: A model type III system in Staphylococcus epidermidis relies upon the activities of two degradosome-associated nucleases, PNPase and RNase J2, to mount a successful defense.
source: Here, we demonstrate that a model type III system in Staphylococcus epidermidis relies upon the activities of two degradosome-associated nucleases, PNPase and RNase J2, to mount a successful defense.
evidence: This is the main finding of the manuscript supported by genetic, molecular, and biochemical analyses presented in the results section.

claim: PNPase promotes crRNA maturation.
source: Genetic, molecular, and biochemical analyses reveal that PNPase promotes crRNA maturation, and both nucleases are required for efficient clearance of phage-derived nucleic acids.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2, where deletion of pnp leads to accumulation of intermediate crRNAs.

claim: Both PNPase and RNase J2 are required for efficient clearance of phage-derived nucleic acids.
source: Genetic, molecular, and biochemical analyses reveal that PNPase promotes crRNA maturation, and both nucleases are required for efficient clearance of phage-derived nucleic acids.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR and qRT-PCR data in Figure 4 showing accumulation of phage nucleic acids in mutant strains.

claim: RNase J2 is essential for immunity against diverse mobile genetic elements originating from plasmid and phage.
source: Furthermore, functional assays show that RNase J2 is essential for immunity against diverse mobile genetic elements originating from plasmid and phage.
evidence: This is supported by functional assays in Figure 3 showing loss of immunity in ΔrnjB mutants against plasmid pG0400 and phages CNPx and Andhra.

claim: Nearly all known archaea and about half of bacteria possess CRISPR-Cas systems.
source: Nearly all known archaea and about half of bacteria possess adaptive immune systems composed of clusters of regularly-interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPRs) and CRISPR-associated (Cas) proteins (Makarova et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Makarova et al., 2015.

claim: CRISPR-Cas systems utilize small CRISPR RNAs (crRNAs) to recognize and destroy prokaryotic viruses (phages).
source: CRISPR-Cas systems utilize small CRISPR RNAs (crRNAs) to recognize and destroy prokaryotic viruses (phages) (Barrangou et al., 2007; Brouns et al., 2008) and other mobile genetic elements (Bikard et al., 2012; Marraffini and Sontheimer, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Barrangou et al., 2007 and Brouns et al., 2008.

claim: CRISPR-Cas systems can recognize and destroy other mobile genetic elements.
source: CRISPR-Cas systems utilize small CRISPR RNAs (crRNAs) to recognize and destroy prokaryotic viruses (phages) (Barrangou et al., 2007; Brouns et al., 2008) and other mobile genetic elements (Bikard et al., 2012; Marraffini and Sontheimer, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Bikard et al., 2012 and Marraffini and Sontheimer, 2008.

claim: The CRISPR-Cas immune response occurs in three steps: adaptation, crRNA biogenesis, and interference.
source: The CRISPR-Cas immune response occurs in three steps: adaptation, crRNA biogenesis, and interference (reviewed in Klompe and Sternberg, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Klompe and Sternberg, 2018.

claim: During adaptation, Cas proteins capture short segments of foreign nucleic acids (24–40 nucleotides in length) and integrate them as 'spacers' into the CRISPR locus.
source: During adaptation, Cas proteins capture short segments of foreign nucleic acids (24–40 nucleotides (nts) in length) and integrate them as 'spacers' into the CRISPR locus in between repeat sequences of similar lengths (Mojica et al., 2005; Yosef et al., 2012) in order to record a molecular memory of past invaders.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Mojica et al., 2005 and Yosef et al., 2012.

claim: During crRNA biogenesis, the repeats and spacers are transcribed into a long precursor crRNA, which is subsequently processed to generate mature crRNAs.
source: During crRNA biogenesis, the repeats and spacers are transcribed into a long precursor crRNA, which is subsequently processed to generate mature crRNAs that each contain a single spacer sequence.
evidence: This is a general description of crRNA biogenesis supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Mature crRNAs combine with one or more Cas proteins to form an effector complex.
source: Mature crRNAs combine with one or more Cas proteins to form an effector complex, which during interference, senses and degrades 'protospacers', invading nucleic acids complementary to the crRNA.
evidence: This is a general description of effector complex formation supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: The current classification scheme divides CRISPR-Cas systems into two classes, six types (I-VI), and dozens of subtypes.
source: Accordingly, the current classification scheme divides these systems into two classes, six types (I-VI), and dozens of subtypes (Koonin et al., 2017; Makarova et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Koonin et al., 2017 and Makarova et al., 2015.

claim: Class one systems (types I, III, and IV) encode multi-subunit effector complexes.
source: Class one systems (types I, III, and IV) encode multi-subunit effector complexes, while Class two systems (types II, V, and VI) possess single subunit effectors.
evidence: This is a classification statement supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Class two systems (types II, V, and VI) possess single subunit effectors.
source: Class one systems (types I, III, and IV) encode multi-subunit effector complexes, while Class two systems (types II, V, and VI) possess single subunit effectors.
evidence: This is a classification statement supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Class one systems are more widespread in nature than Class two systems.
source: Although Class two systems have garnered significant attention over the past decade due to their versatile genetic applications (Klompe and Sternberg, 2018), Class one systems are more widespread in nature, and of these, type III systems are believed to be the most closely related to the common ancestor from which all other CRISPR types have evolved (Mohanraju et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Klompe and Sternberg, 2018.

claim: Type III systems are believed to be the most closely related to the common ancestor from which all other CRISPR types have evolved.
source: Although Class two systems have garnered significant attention over the past decade due to their versatile genetic applications (Klompe and Sternberg, 2018), Class one systems are more widespread in nature, and of these, type III systems are believed to be the most closely related to the common ancestor from which all other CRISPR types have evolved (Mohanraju et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Mohanraju et al., 2016.

claim: Staphylococcus epidermidis RP62a harbors a well-established model type III-A CRISPR-Cas system.
source: Staphylococcus epidermidis RP62a harbors a well-established model type III-A CRISPR-Cas system (Figure 1A), here onward referred to as CRISPR-Cas10.
evidence: This statement is supported by Figure 1A showing the CRISPR-Cas10 system and citations to prior work.

claim: The CRISPR-Cas10 system encodes three spacers and nine CRISPR-associated proteins.
source: This system encodes three spacers (spc) and nine CRISPR-associated proteins (Cas and Csm) that can prevent the transfer of a conjugative plasmid (Marraffini and Sontheimer, 2010) and stave off phage infection (Maniv et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by Figure 1A and citations to Marraffini and Sontheimer, 2010 and Maniv et al., 2016.

claim: The CRISPR-Cas10 system can prevent the transfer of a conjugative plasmid.
source: This system encodes three spacers (spc) and nine CRISPR-associated proteins (Cas and Csm) that can prevent the transfer of a conjugative plasmid (Marraffini and Sontheimer, 2010) and stave off phage infection (Maniv et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Marraffini and Sontheimer, 2010.

claim: The CRISPR-Cas10 system can stave off phage infection.
source: This system encodes three spacers (spc) and nine CRISPR-associated proteins (Cas and Csm) that can prevent the transfer of a conjugative plasmid (Marraffini and Sontheimer, 2010) and stave off phage infection (Maniv et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Maniv et al., 2016.

claim: The Cas6 endoribonuclease cleaves the precursor crRNA within repeat sequences to generate 71 nt intermediate crRNAs.
source: Defense begins with crRNA biogenesis (Figure 1B), during which the Cas6 endoribonuclease cleaves the precursor crRNA within repeat sequences to generate 71 nt intermediate crRNAs (Hatoum-Aslan et al., 2011; Hatoum-Aslan et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by Figure 1B and citations to Hatoum-Aslan et al., 2011 and Hatoum-Aslan et al., 2014.

claim: Intermediate crRNAs are subsequently trimmed on their 3'-ends to generate mature species that range in length from 31 to 43 nts.
source: These intermediates are subsequently trimmed on their 3'-ends to generate mature species that range in length from 31 to 43 nts (Hatoum-Aslan et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Hatoum-Aslan et al., 2013.

claim: Mature crRNAs combine with Cas10, Csm2, Csm3, Csm4, and Csm5 to form the Cas10-Csm effector complex.
source: Mature crRNAs combine with Cas10, Csm2, Csm3, Csm4, and Csm5 to form the Cas10-Csm effector complex (Hatoum-Aslan et al., 2013) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This statement is supported by Figure 1C and citation to Hatoum-Aslan et al., 2013.

claim: The Cas10-Csm effector complex, in conjunction with the accessory ribonuclease Csm6, wage a two-pronged attack against foreign DNA and RNA.
source: During interference, this complex, in conjunction with the accessory ribonuclease Csm6, wage a two-pronged attack against foreign DNA and RNA.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge and citations in the manuscript.

claim: Interference is triggered by the binding of the crRNA to the targeted transcript.
source: Interference is triggered by the binding of the crRNA to the targeted transcript (Goldberg et al., 2014), an event that leads to the activation of at least three nucleases: Cas10 cleaves the non-template (coding) DNA strand (Samai et al., 2015), each Csm3 subunit slices RNA within the protospacer region (Samai et al., 2015; Staals et al., 2014; Tamulaitis et al., 2014), and Csm6 degrades nonspecific transcripts in the vicinity (Foster et al., 2018; Jiang et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Goldberg et al., 2014.

claim: Cas10 cleaves the non-template (coding) DNA strand.
source: Interference is triggered by the binding of the crRNA to the targeted transcript (Goldberg et al., 2014), an event that leads to the activation of at least three nucleases: Cas10 cleaves the non-template (coding) DNA strand (Samai et al., 2015), each Csm3 subunit slices RNA within the protospacer region (Samai et al., 2015; Staals et al., 2014; Tamulaitis et al., 2014), and Csm6 degrades nonspecific transcripts in the vicinity (Foster et al., 2018; Jiang et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Samai et al., 2015.

claim: Each Csm3 subunit slices RNA within the protospacer region.
source: Interference is triggered by the binding of the crRNA to the targeted transcript (Goldberg et al., 2014), an event that leads to the activation of at least three nucleases: Cas10 cleaves the non-template (coding) DNA strand (Samai et al., 2015), each Csm3 subunit slices RNA within the protospacer region (Samai et al., 2015; Staals et al., 2014; Tamulaitis et al., 2014), and Csm6 degrades nonspecific transcripts in the vicinity (Foster et al., 2018; Jiang et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Samai et al., 2015; Staals et al., 2014; and Tamulaitis et al., 2014.

claim: Csm6 degrades nonspecific transcripts in the vicinity.
source: Interference is triggered by the binding of the crRNA to the targeted transcript (Goldberg et al., 2014), an event that leads to the activation of at least three nucleases: Cas10 cleaves the non-template (coding) DNA strand (Samai et al., 2015), each Csm3 subunit slices RNA within the protospacer region (Samai et al., 2015; Staals et al., 2014; Tamulaitis et al., 2014), and Csm6 degrades nonspecific transcripts in the vicinity (Foster et al., 2018; Jiang et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Foster et al., 2018 and Jiang et al., 2016.

claim: In related type III-A systems, target RNA binding triggers the cleavage of non-specific single-stranded DNA by the HD domain of Cas10.
source: In related type III-A systems, target RNA binding has also been shown to trigger two additional functions of Cas10: the cleavage of non-specific single-stranded DNA by its HD domain (Kazlauskiene et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2017), and the generation of cyclic oligoadenylates by its Palm polymerase domain (Kazlauskiene et al., 2017; Niewoehner et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Kazlauskiene et al., 2016 and Liu et al., 2017.

claim: In related type III-A systems, target RNA binding triggers the generation of cyclic oligoadenylates by the Palm polymerase domain of Cas10.
source: In related type III-A systems, target RNA binding has also been shown to trigger two additional functions of Cas10: the cleavage of non-specific single-stranded DNA by its HD domain (Kazlauskiene et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2017), and the generation of cyclic oligoadenylates by its Palm polymerase domain (Kazlauskiene et al., 2017; Niewoehner et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Kazlauskiene et al., 2017 and Niewoehner et al., 2017.

claim: Cyclic oligoadenylates act as second messengers which bind and further stimulate Csm6.
source: The cyclic oligoadenylates act as second messengers which bind and further stimulate Csm6, thus accelerating its activity near the site of foreign nucleic acid detection.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the field and citations in the manuscript.

claim: The combined activities of the Cas and Csm nucleases, together with the high tolerance for mismatches between the crRNA and protospacer pairing, contribute to a powerful immune response that can lead to phage extinction with a single targeting spacer.
source: The combined activities of the Cas and Csm nucleases, together with the high tolerance for mismatches between the crRNA and protospacer pairing (Pyenson et al., 2017), contribute to a particularly powerful immune response that can lead to phage extinction with a single targeting spacer (Bari et al., 2017; Pyenson et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Pyenson et al., 2017 and Bari et al., 2017.

claim: The Cas10-Csm complex, when expressed in its native S. epidermidis host, co-purifies with several cellular nucleases in trace amounts.
source: Indeed, our previous work showed that the Cas10-Csm complex, when expressed in its native S. epidermidis host, co-purifies with several cellular nucleases in trace amounts (Walker et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Walker et al., 2017.

claim: In a reconstituted system, Csm5 can bind and stimulate PNPase.
source: Furthermore, in a reconstituted system, Csm5 can bind and stimulate one of these nucleases, PNPase (polynucleotide phosphorylase), a highly-conserved enzyme that is responsible for the processing and degradation of cellular RNAs in bacteria and eukaryotes (Cameron et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Cameron et al., 2018.

claim: PNPase is a highly-conserved enzyme that is responsible for the processing and degradation of cellular RNAs in bacteria and eukaryotes.
source: Furthermore, in a reconstituted system, Csm5 can bind and stimulate one of these nucleases, PNPase (polynucleotide phosphorylase), a highly-conserved enzyme that is responsible for the processing and degradation of cellular RNAs in bacteria and eukaryotes (Cameron et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Cameron et al., 2018.

claim: In bacteria, PNPase can act independently, or associate with other enzymes to form an RNA degrading machine called the degradosome.
source: In bacteria, PNPase can act independently, or associate with other enzymes (including nucleases and helicases) to form an RNA degrading machine called the degradosome (Cameron et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Cameron et al., 2018.

claim: RNase J2 co-purifies with the Cas10-Csm complex.
source: To test this, we deleted the genes encoding PNPase and Ribonuclease (RNase) J2, a second degradosome nuclease that co-purifies with the Cas10-Csm complex (Walker et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Walker et al., 2017.

claim: PNPase is required for efficient crRNA maturation, but RNase J2 is not.
source: We discovered that PNPase is indeed required for efficient crRNA maturation, but RNase J2 is not.
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data in Figure 2 showing crRNA maturation defects in Δpnp but not ΔrnjB mutants.

claim: While PNPase appears to be dispensable for CRISPR-Cas10 function, RNase J2 is essential to block the transfer of a conjugative plasmid and defend against two unrelated phages.
source: In contrast, while PNPase appears to be dispensable for CRISPR-Cas10 function, RNase J2 is essential to block the transfer of a conjugative plasmid and defend against two unrelated phages, therefore establishing a general requirement for RNase J2 in CRISPR-Cas10 immunity.
evidence: This statement is supported by functional assays in Figure 3 showing immunity defects in ΔrnjB but not Δpnp mutants.

claim: RNase J2 promotes cellular RNA degradation by binding and stimulating the ribonuclease activity of its paralog RNase J1.
source: It has been well documented by others that RNase J2 promotes cellular RNA degradation by binding and stimulating the ribonuclease activity of its paralog RNase J1 (Hausmann et al., 2017; Linder et al., 2014; Mathy et al., 2007; Mathy et al., 2010; Raj et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hausmann et al., 2017; Linder et al., 2014; Mathy et al., 2007; Mathy et al., 2010; and Raj et al., 2018.

claim: S. epidermidis RNase J2 promotes robust DNA degradation through the same mechanism by which it promotes RNA degradation.
source: Here, we show that S. epidermidis RNase J2 also promotes robust DNA degradation through this same mechanism.
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data in Figure 5 showing DNA degradation by RNase J1/J2 complex.

claim: In the Δpnp mutant, 50.6 (±3.0) % of complex-associated crRNAs exist in the intermediate state.
source: when purified from wild-type background, 6.2 (±2.4) % of complex-associated crRNAs exists in the intermediate state, whereas in the Δpnp mutant, intermediates represent 50.6 (±3.0) % of all crRNAs in the complex (Figure 2C and Figure 2—source data 1), indicating that PNPase is indeed required for efficient crRNA maturation.
evidence: This statement is supported by quantitative data from Figure 2C and Figure 2—source data 1.

claim: In wild-type background, 6.2 (±2.4) % of complex-associated crRNAs exist in the intermediate state.
source: when purified from wild-type background, 6.2 (±2.4) % of complex-associated crRNAs exists in the intermediate state, whereas in the Δpnp mutant, intermediates represent 50.6 (±3.0) % of all crRNAs in the complex (Figure 2C and Figure 2—source data 1), indicating that PNPase is indeed required for efficient crRNA maturation.
evidence: This statement is supported by quantitative data from Figure 2C and Figure 2—source data 1.

claim: Complex formation remains unaffected in the Δpnp mutant.
source: While complex formation remained unaffected in the Δpnp mutant (Figure 2A), we observed that the crRNA sizes associated with these complexes differed dramatically from the wild-type (Figure 2B)
evidence: This statement is supported by Figure 2A showing intact Cas10-Csm complexes in the Δpnp mutant.

claim: Cas10-Csm remains intact when expressed in the ΔrnjB background.
source: We observed that Cas10-Csm remains intact when expressed in the ΔrnjB background (Figure 2A), and the crRNA size distribution is similar to that observed in the wild-type control (Figure 2B and C and Figure 2—source data 1), indicating that RNase J2 is unlikely to play a significant role in crRNA maturation.
evidence: This statement is supported by Figure 2A showing intact Cas10-Csm complexes in the ΔrnjB mutant.

claim: The crRNA size distribution in the ΔrnjB mutant is similar to that observed in the wild-type control.
source: We observed that Cas10-Csm remains intact when expressed in the ΔrnjB background (Figure 2A), and the crRNA size distribution is similar to that observed in the wild-type control (Figure 2B and C and Figure 2—source data 1), indicating that RNase J2 is unlikely to play a significant role in crRNA maturation.
evidence: This statement is supported by Figure 2B and C showing similar crRNA distributions in ΔrnjB and wild-type.

claim: The ΔpnpΔrnjB double-mutant exhibits a maturation defect similar to that observed in the Δpnp single mutant.
source: To confirm, we also created the ΔpnpΔrnjB double-mutant (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and found that it exhibits a maturation defect similar to that observed in the Δpnp single mutant (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This statement is supported by Figure 2B and C showing similar crRNA maturation defects in Δpnp and ΔpnpΔrnjB mutants.

claim: The wild-type LM1680 strain bearing the empty vector showed a conjugation efficiency in the 10−3 range.
source: Indeed, the controls behaved consistently with previous results (Hatoum-Aslan et al., 2013), where the wild-type LM1680 strain bearing the empty vector (pC194) showed a conjugation efficiency in the 10−3 range, while this same strain harboring pcrispr-cas exhibited an efficiency in the 10−7 range (Figure 3B and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by Figure 3B and Figure 3—source data 1 showing conjugation efficiency data.

claim: The wild-type LM1680 strain harboring pcrispr-cas exhibited a conjugation efficiency in the 10−7 range.
source: Indeed, the controls behaved consistently with previous results (Hatoum-Aslan et al., 2013), where the wild-type LM1680 strain bearing the empty vector (pC194) showed a conjugation efficiency in the 10−3 range, while this same strain harboring pcrispr-cas exhibited an efficiency in the 10−7 range (Figure 3B and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by Figure 3B and Figure 3—source data 1 showing conjugation efficiency data.

claim: The Δpnp/pcrispr-cas strain had a conjugation efficiency similar to that of the wild-type strain expressing the CRISPR-Cas10 system.
source: Interestingly, despite the maturation defect in Δpnp/pcrispr-cas, this strain had a conjugation efficiency similar to that of the wild-type strain expressing the CRISPR-Cas10 system, suggesting that PNPase is dispensable for anti-plasmid immunity.
evidence: This statement is supported by Figure 3B showing similar conjugation efficiencies for wild-type and Δpnp strains with pcrispr-cas.

claim: ΔrnjB/pcrispr-cas exhibited a significant defect in immunity, with a conjugation efficiency similar to that of the negative control.
source: In contrast, ΔrnjB/pcrispr-cas exhibited a significant defect in immunity, with a conjugation efficiency similar to that of the negative control.
evidence: This statement is supported by Figure 3B showing high conjugation efficiency in ΔrnjB/pcrispr-cas similar to the negative control.

claim: CRISPR-Cas10 appears to retain a modest level of anti-plasmid immunity in the double mutant.
source: Interestingly, CRISPR-Cas10 appears to retain a modest level of anti-plasmid immunity in the double mutant, resulting in a conjugation efficiency that is an order of magnitude lower than that observed in the absence of pcrispr-cas (compare 2.2 × 10−4 to 2.6 × 10−3).
evidence: This statement is supported by Figure 3B showing conjugation efficiency data for the double mutant.

claim: Complementation strains containing a copy of rnjB on pcrispr-cas exhibited conjugation efficiencies similar to those of the wild-type strain bearing pcrispr-cas.
source: Importantly, complementation strains containing a copy of rnjB on pcrispr-cas (a plasmid called pcrispr-cas-rnjB) exhibited conjugation efficiencies similar to those of the wild-type strain bearing pcrispr-cas (Figure 3B and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by Figure 3B and Figure 3—source data 1 showing conjugation efficiency data for complementation strains.

claim: When the LM1680/pcrispr-cas strain is challenged with CNPx, not a single plaque is visible.
source: However, when the LM1680/pcrispr-cas strain is challenged with CNPx, not a single plaque is visible, in agreement with the robust anti-phage immunity previously reported for this system (Bari et al., 2017; Pyenson et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by Figure 3D showing no plaques for LM1680/pcrispr-cas challenged with CNPx, and citations to Bari et al., 2017 and Pyenson et al., 2017.

claim: The Δpnp strain appeared to perform like wild-type in the CNPx phage challenge assay.
source: Importantly, when we challenged the mutant strains with CNPx, we observed a significant defect, even more pronounced than that seen for anti-plasmid immunity: While the Δpnp strain appeared to perform like wild-type, the ΔrnjB and ΔpnpΔrnjB mutations abolished CRISPR-Cas10 function altogether.
evidence: This statement is supported by Figure 3D showing no plaques for Δpnp strain challenged with CNPx.

claim: The ΔrnjB and ΔpnpΔrnjB mutations abolished CRISPR-Cas10 function in the CNPx phage challenge assay.
source: Importantly, when we challenged the mutant strains with CNPx, we observed a significant defect, even more pronounced than that seen for anti-plasmid immunity: While the Δpnp strain appeared to perform like wild-type, the ΔrnjB and ΔpnpΔrnjB mutations abolished CRISPR-Cas10 function altogether.
evidence: This statement is supported by Figure 3D showing high plaque counts for ΔrnjB and ΔpnpΔrnjB strains challenged with CNPx.

claim: Returning rnjB to the defective mutants on pcrispr-cas-rnjB restored full immunity against CNPx.
source: In addition, returning rnjB to these defective mutants on pcrispr-cas-rnjB restored full immunity against CNPx.
evidence: This statement is supported by Figure 3D showing no plaques for complementation strains challenged with CNPx.

claim: When transformed with pcrispr-spcA2, only the wild-type and Δpnp strains gain complete immunity to Andhra.
source: However, when transformed with pcrispr-spcA2, only the wild-type and Δpnp strains gain complete immunity to Andhra, while the ΔrnjB and ΔpnpΔrnjB strains remain as sensitive to Andhra as the corresponding negative controls without the pcrispr-spcA2 plasmid.
evidence: This statement is supported by Figure 3F showing no plaques for wild-type and Δpnp strains with pcrispr-spcA2, but high plaque counts for ΔrnjB and ΔpnpΔrnjB strains.

claim: The ΔrnjB and ΔpnpΔrnjB strains remain as sensitive to Andhra as the corresponding negative controls without the pcrispr-spcA2 plasmid.
source: However, when transformed with pcrispr-spcA2, only the wild-type and Δpnp strains gain complete immunity to Andhra, while the ΔrnjB and ΔpnpΔrnjB strains remain as sensitive to Andhra as the corresponding negative controls without the pcrispr-spcA2 plasmid.
evidence: This statement is supported by Figure 3F showing similar high plaque counts for ΔrnjB and ΔpnpΔrnjB strains with and without pcrispr-spcA2.

claim: The Δpnp/pcrispr-spcA2 strain showed a significant (~10 fold) accumulation of phage RNA and DNA.
source: Interestingly, the Δpnp/pcrispr-spcA2 strain showed a significant (~10 fold) accumulation of phage RNA and DNA, but not as high as that observed in the negative control strain devoid of pcrispr-spcA2.
evidence: This statement is supported by Figure 4B and C showing phage RNA and DNA accumulation in the Δpnp/pcrispr-spcA2 strain.

claim: The ΔrnjB/pcrispr-spcA2 and ΔpnpΔrnjB/pcrispr-spcA2 strains showed significant accumulation of phage-derived DNA and transcripts when compared to the wild-type strain bearing pcrispr-spcA2.
source: We also tested the ΔrnjB/pcrispr-spcA2 and ΔpnpΔrnjB/pcrispr-spcA2 strains, and in agreement with their impaired CRISPR-Cas10 function, both strains showed significant accumulation of phage-derived DNA and transcripts when compared to the wild-type strain bearing pcrispr-spcA2.
evidence: This statement is supported by Figure 4B and C showing phage RNA and DNA accumulation in ΔrnjB/pcrispr-spcA2 and ΔpnpΔrnjB/pcrispr-spcA2 strains.

claim: The double mutant showed a greater defect in the clearance of phage nucleic acids than the ΔrnjB single mutant.
source: Notably, the double mutant showed a greater defect in the clearance of phage nucleic acids than the ΔrnjB single mutant, thus confirming the contribution of PNPase towards phage nucleic acid degradation.
evidence: This statement is supported by Figure 4B and C showing higher phage RNA and DNA accumulation in the double mutant compared to the ΔrnjB single mutant.

claim: The relative amounts of phage nucleic acids in the ΔrnjB/pcrispr-spcA2 and ΔpnpΔrnjB/pcrispr-spcA2 strains significantly exceeded those seen in the wild-type strain lacking pcrispr-spcA2.
source: One additional observation in this data was striking: The relative amounts of phage nucleic acids in the ΔrnjB/pcrispr-spcA2 and ΔpnpΔrnjB/pcrispr-spcA2 strains significantly exceeded those seen in the wild-type strain lacking pcrispr-spcA2.
evidence: This statement is supported by Figure 4B and C showing higher phage RNA and DNA levels in mutant strains with pcrispr-spcA2 compared to wild-type without pcrispr-spcA2.

claim: Δpnp and ΔrnjB mutants accumulated over 400 and 1300 times more phage DNA, respectively, by 30 min post-infection compared to wild-type.
source: Strikingly, Δpnp and ΔrnjB mutants accumulated over 400 and 1300 times more phage DNA, respectively, by this same time point.
evidence: This statement is supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1 showing phage DNA accumulation in Δpnp and ΔrnjB mutants without pcrispr-spcA2.

claim: PNPase and RNase J2 facilitate the restriction of phage DNA amplification within the cell, even in the absence of a targeting CRISPR system.
source: These data indicate that PNPase and RNase J2 facilitate the restriction of phage DNA amplification within the cell, even in the absence of a targeting CRISPR system.
evidence: This statement is supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1 showing increased phage DNA accumulation in Δpnp and ΔrnjB mutants without pcrispr-spcA2.

claim: Bacterial PNPase homologs can degrade DNA substrates.
source: Although PNPase is most well-known for its ribonuclease activity (Cameron et al., 2018; Hui et al., 2014), we and others have recently shown that bacterial PNPase homologs can also degrade DNA substrates (Cardenas et al., 2009; Walker et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Cardenas et al., 2009 and Walker et al., 2017.

claim: Studies on bacterial RNase J homologs have strictly reported ribonuclease activities in these enzymes.
source: In contrast, studies on bacterial RNase J homologs have strictly reported ribonuclease activities in these enzymes (Hausmann et al., 2017; Linder et al., 2014; Mathy et al., 2007; Mathy et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hausmann et al., 2017; Linder et al., 2014; Mathy et al., 2007; and Mathy et al., 2010.

claim: Two archaeal RNase J homologs were shown to catalyze the cleavage of single-stranded DNA.
source: One exception seems to be in two archaeal RNase J homologs, which were shown to catalyze the cleavage of single-stranded DNA (Levy et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Levy et al., 2011.

claim: RNase J1 exhibits Mn2+-dependent ribonuclease activity that leaves behind a single small cleavage product, implying 5'−3' exonuclease activity.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Hausmann et al., 2017; Mathy et al., 2010), we observed insignificant nuclease activity in RNase J2, and Mn2+-dependent ribonuclease activity in RNase J1 that leaves behind a single small cleavage product, implying 5'−3' exonuclease activity.
evidence: This statement is supported by Figure 5C showing RNA cleavage by RNase J1 and citations to Hausmann et al., 2017 and Mathy et al., 2010.

claim: RNase J1's ribonuclease activity appeared more pronounced when RNase J1 was combined with RNase J2 in a 1:1 ratio.
source: Furthermore, this function appeared more pronounced when RNase J1 was combined with RNase J2 in a 1:1 ratio.
evidence: This statement is supported by Figure 5C and D showing enhanced RNA cleavage when RNase J1 and J2 are combined.

claim: RNase J1 alone could only degrade 23 (±14) % of the RNA substrate during a 20 min incubation period.
source: whereas RNase J1 alone could only degrade 23 (±14) % of the substrate during a 20 min incubation period, the combined proteins eliminated 95 (±1) % of the substrate in the same amount of time (Figure 5D and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by Figure 5D and Figure 5—source data 1 showing quantification of RNA cleavage.

claim: The combined RNase J1 and J2 proteins eliminated 95 (±1) % of the RNA substrate in 20 min.
source: whereas RNase J1 alone could only degrade 23 (±14) % of the substrate during a 20 min incubation period, the combined proteins eliminated 95 (±1) % of the substrate in the same amount of time (Figure 5D and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by Figure 5D and Figure 5—source data 1 showing quantification of RNA cleavage.

claim: The catalytically-dead RNase J1 mutant combined with RNase J2 showed no nucleolytic activity on RNA.
source: Furthermore, the catalytically-dead RNase J1 mutant combined with RNase J2 showed no nucleolytic activity, confirming that the nuclease active site in the J1/J2 complex originates from RNase J1.
evidence: This statement is supported by Figure 5C showing no RNA cleavage by dJ1/J2 complex.

claim: A striking Mn2+-dependent DNase activity was observed when RNase J1 and J2 were combined.
source: While we detected little/no nuclease activity from each enzyme alone, a striking Mn2+-dependent DNase activity was observed when the enzymes were combined, which again resulted in a single small cleavage product indicative of a 5'−3' exonuclease function.
evidence: This statement is supported by Figure 5E showing DNA cleavage by RNase J1/J2 complex.

claim: RNase J1 alone cleaved 17 (±8) % of the DNA substrate after 5 min.
source: For example, while RNase J1 alone cleaved 17 (±8) % of the DNA substrate after 5 min, the J1/J2 complex had already degraded 99 (±1) % of the substrate in the same amount of time.
evidence: This statement is supported by Figure 5F and Figure 5—source data 2 showing quantification of DNA cleavage.

claim: The RNase J1/J2 complex degraded 99 (±1) % of the DNA substrate in 5 min.
source: For example, while RNase J1 alone cleaved 17 (±8) % of the DNA substrate after 5 min, the J1/J2 complex had already degraded 99 (±1) % of the substrate in the same amount of time.
evidence: This statement is supported by Figure 5F and Figure 5—source data 2 showing quantification of DNA cleavage.

claim: Cleavage of double-stranded circular or linear DNA by RNase J homologs could not be detected.
source: While cleavage of double-stranded circular or linear DNA could not be detected (Figure 5G), we observed degradation of the single-stranded circular DNA by RNase J1, an activity that is significantly stimulated when combined with RNase J2 (Figure 5H).
evidence: This statement is supported by Figure 5G showing no cleavage of double-stranded DNA.

claim: Degradation of single-stranded circular DNA by RNase J1 is significantly stimulated when combined with RNase J2.
source: While cleavage of double-stranded circular or linear DNA could not be detected (Figure 5G), we observed degradation of the single-stranded circular DNA by RNase J1, an activity that is significantly stimulated when combined with RNase J2 (Figure 5H).
evidence: This statement is supported by Figure 5H showing enhanced cleavage of single-stranded circular DNA by RNase J1/J2 complex.

claim: The DNA endonuclease active site resides within RNase J1.
source: Again, the catalytically-dead RNase J1 completely lost this function, indicating that the DNA endonuclease active site resides within RNase J1.
evidence: This statement is supported by Figure 5H showing no DNA cleavage by dJ1/J2 complex.

claim: Csm5 binds directly to PNPase and stimulates its nucleolytic activity in a purified system.
source: We previously showed that Csm5 binds directly to PNPase and stimulates its nucleolytic activity in a purified system (Walker et al., 2017), thus providing mechanisms for PNPase's recruitment and regulation during crRNA maturation and interference in vivo.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Walker et al., 2017.

claim: PNPase has been shown to bind RNase J1.
source: Since PNPase has been shown to bind RNase J1 (Raj et al., 2018; Roux et al., 2011), and since RNases J1 and J2 exist as a complex in the cell (Mathy et al., 2010), one possible mechanism for the recruitment of RNase J2 to the site of CRISPR interference could be through its connection with PNPase.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Raj et al., 2018 and Roux et al., 2011.

claim: RNases J1 and J2 exist as a complex in the cell.
source: Since PNPase has been shown to bind RNase J1 (Raj et al., 2018; Roux et al., 2011), and since RNases J1 and J2 exist as a complex in the cell (Mathy et al., 2010), one possible mechanism for the recruitment of RNase J2 to the site of CRISPR interference could be through its connection with PNPase.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Mathy et al., 2010.

claim: There have been two reports of phage-encoded proteins that specifically inhibit RNase E, a central subunit of the degradosome in gram negative organisms.
source: Interestingly, there have been two reports of phage-encoded proteins that specifically inhibit RNase E, a central subunit of the degradosome in gram negative organisms (Van den Bossche et al., 2016; Hui et al., 2014; Marchand et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Van den Bossche et al., 2016; Hui et al., 2014; and Marchand et al., 2001.

claim: S. epidermidis Cas10 cleaves only the coding DNA strand in the protospacer region, leaving the non-coding strand unharmed.
source: Furthermore, S. epidermidis Cas10 (SeCas10) cleaves only the coding DNA strand in the protospacer region, leaving the non-coding strand unharmed (Samai et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Samai et al., 2015 and Wang et al., 2019.

claim: Cas10 homologs in related type III-A systems exhibit nonspecific DNA endonuclease activity.
source: Although Cas10 homologs in related type III-A systems exhibit nonspecific DNA endonuclease activity (Kazlauskiene et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2017), this function in SeCas10 has yet to be demonstrated.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Kazlauskiene et al., 2016 and Liu et al., 2017.

claim: RNase J homologs catalyze endonuclease activity, as well as 5'−3' exonucleolytic activity.
source: It is worthwhile mentioning that while PNPase exhibits 3'−5' exonuclease activity on DNA and RNA substrates (Cameron et al., 2018; Cardenas et al., 2009; Walker et al., 2017), RNase J homologs catalyze endonuclease activity, as well as 5'−3' exonucleolytic activity, a function only recently thought to be non-existent in bacteria (Hausmann et al., 2017; Linder et al., 2014; Mathy et al., 2007; Mathy et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hausmann et al., 2017; Linder et al., 2014; Mathy et al., 2007; and Mathy et al., 2010.

claim: In a type II CRISPR-Cas system in Streptococcus pyogenes, both the crRNA and the tracrRNA are processed by the host-encoded RNase III.
source: The earliest example of such a collaboration was seen in a type II CRISPR-Cas system in Streptococcus pyogenes, in which both the crRNA and the tracrRNA are processed by the host-encoded RNase III (Deltcheva et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Deltcheva et al., 2011.

claim: A type III-Bv system in Synechocystis 6803, which lacks a Cas6 homolog, was found to utilize the host-encoded RNase E to catalyze crRNA processing.
source: In a more recent example, a type III-Bv (variant) system in Synechocystis 6803, which lacks a Cas6 homolog, was found to utilize the host-encoded RNase E to catalyze crRNA processing (Behler et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Behler et al., 2018.

claim: A CRISPR-like element in Listeria monocytogenes devoid of its own cas genes was shown to rely upon a type I CRISPR-Cas system and host-encoded PNPase for small RNA processing and interference.
source: In yet a third example, a CRISPR-like element in Listeria monocytogenes devoid of its own cas genes, was shown to rely upon a type I CRISPR-Cas system and host-encoded PNPase for small RNA processing and interference (Sesto et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Sesto et al., 2014.

claim: Diverse CRISPR-Cas types have independently evolved different mechanisms to tap into the arsenal of nucleolytic enzymes that bacteria utilize for routine functions.
source: From these seemingly disparate observations, perhaps a common theme is beginning to emerge in which diverse CRISPR-Cas types have independently evolved different mechanisms to tap into the arsenal of nucleolytic enzymes that bacteria utilize for routine functions, and channel their activities towards defense in the event of a phage infection.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from multiple examples of CRISPR systems utilizing host nucleases.

claim: The latent period for phage Andhra is 35 min.
source: Importantly, the latent period for Andhra was previously determined to be 35 min (Cater et al., 2017), therefore the selected time points all occur within the timeframe of a single infection cycle before the first burst.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Cater et al., 2017.

claim: CNPx is a variant of CNPH82, a temperate phage belonging to the morphological family Siphoviridae.
source: The first, CNPx, is a variant of CNPH82, a temperate phage belonging to the morphological family Siphoviridae (Daniel et al., 2007; Maniv et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Daniel et al., 2007 and Maniv et al., 2016.

claim: Andhra is a lytic phage belonging to the morphological family Podoviridae.
source: Andhra is a lytic phage belonging to the morphological family Podoviridae, and spcA2 targets its DNA polymerase (gp09) gene.
evidence: This is a description of phage Andhra supported by established knowledge.

claim: S. epidermidis LM1680 was originally derived from RP62a as a CRISPR 'escape' mutant which harbors a ~ 258,000 nt deletion encompassing the CRISPR locus and flanking regions.
source: S. epidermidis LM1680 was originally derived from RP62a as a CRISPR 'escape' mutant which harbors a ~ 258,000 nt deletion encompassing the CRISPR locus and flanking regions (Jiang et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Jiang et al., 2013.
